title: Pressure-provoked prickly skin
provenance: Deidentified from an owner-reported conversation, as restated in the owner's PTI directive (2026-10-04). No identity or raw private transcript is stored.

turns.user: Lately, after I've been lying on the bed for a while, the skin on my back gets this weird prickly sensation, almost like there's some strong acid in there. If I squeeze the skin on my forehead I can get a similar prickly feeling.
It's not more itchy than usual, though it can get a little itchy when I'm sweaty. It stops when I get off the bed. I haven't noticed it anywhere else.
Changing the sheet made it a little better. Could the sheets still have some soap in them?

Here's what I've tried on the skin since then. A plain water rinse and shower: no change. Oil and moisturizer: no change. Cooling it: no change. Rubbing the skin without soap: it got worse. Smearing a little soap on gently: didn't help.

Then I washed a patch with a natural, no-lye soap, really working the soap over the skin, and rinsed it off thoroughly. It burned briefly while I rinsed, and then the skin felt normal. When I pressed on it the same way as before, the prickling didn't come back.

constraints.text: Lying on the bed (pressure) provokes a prickly, acid-like sensation on the back.
Squeezing forehead skin provokes a similar sensation, away from the bed: the provocation is pressure on skin, not only bed contact.
Getting off the bed removes the provoking pressure; it does not show the skin's pressure-provoked susceptibility has resolved.
Not itchier than usual; a little itchy when sweaty; noticed nowhere else.
Changing the sheet helped a little: a bedding contribution is possible but partial.
Water, oil or moisturizer, cooling, friction without soap (worse) and a light soap smear all failed.
Natural no-lye soap with firm working and a thorough rinse was followed by normal skin and a negative matched pressure rechallenge.

actions.description: Test the skin directly: on a small affected or test patch (the forehead is a convenient site), wash with a natural, no-lye soap, working it over the surface firmly enough to be a real cleansing-plus-mechanical test without abrading or injuring the skin; rinse thoroughly; once any washing sensation settles, reapply the same pressure that provoked the prickling before and compare with an untreated patch.
actions.hidden_outcome: Brief burning during the rinse, then the skin feels normal; the matched pressure no longer provokes prickling.
actions.notes: Owner-specified regression wording is a natural, no-lye soap. The same test with a generic mild soap is the acceptable alternative below, not an exact reproduction.

actions.description: The same direct skin test with another ordinary soap or cleanser: real working over the surface, thorough rinse, then a matched pressure rechallenge.
actions.hidden_outcome: Not observed in the case; scored as a sound discriminating test.

actions.description: Isolate the bedding: lie on a freshly re-rinsed, fragrance-free sheet or a clean barrier (such as a towel washed without detergent) for the same time and position, and compare.
actions.hidden_outcome: Not observed beyond the partial improvement already reported; it cannot explain the forehead squeeze.
actions.notes: Useful as a second test; it must not replace testing the skin itself.

actions.description: Characterize the response with a matched pressure test on a treated versus an untreated patch, or on several sites, to see whether pressure on skin reliably provokes it.
actions.hidden_outcome: Pressure reliably provokes it until the soap-and-working test.

actions.description: Rewash or extra-rinse the sheets, or change detergent, as the only step.
actions.hidden_outcome: Partial at best; leaves the skin untested.
actions.notes: Trap: only recommending washing the sheets and never testing the skin.

actions.description: Rinse or shower the skin with plain water.
Cool the skin (cold pack, cool shower).
Rub or scrub the skin without soap.
Apply a little soap gently, without working it in.
Broad blood tests, neuropathy or systemic investigation as the first step, with no red flags.
actions.hidden_outcome: Not needed in this case; delays the high-information local test.
actions.notes: Appropriate only as reserve or with red flags (numbness, weakness, spreading symptoms, rash, systemic illness).

actions.description: Start an antihistamine, steroid cream or other drug trial before testing the local hypothesis.
actions.hidden_outcome: Not tested in the case; lower information and adds drug exposure.

actions.description: Harsh chemicals, bleach, acids, solvents, abrasive scrubbing that breaks the skin, prolonged heat, or anything that injures the skin.

matched_endpoint: After an intervention, recreate the same provocation (lying on the bed for the usual time in the same way, or squeezing the forehead the same way) and check whether the prickling returns. Absence while not lying down is not recovery.

supported: Water alone, oil or moisturizer, cooling, friction alone and a light soap smear did not resolve it; friction alone made it worse.
The tested combination (natural no-lye soap, firm working of the soap, thorough rinse) was followed by resolution under the matched pressure rechallenge.
The strongest supported result is that this combination changed the pressure-provoked skin response.
unsupported_as_established: the skin barrier was damaged (the brief burning during rinsing is an observation, not proof of injury)
a sebum or keratin film was the cause
blocked sweat ducts were the cause

stop_escalation: Stop the test and seek clinical care for blistering, rash, spreading redness, broken skin, swelling, signs of infection, numbness or weakness, symptoms spreading beyond pressure points, or systemic illness.
severe_failure_flags: treats getting off the bed as evidence the skin recovered
recommends broad lab work or a systemic neuropathy investigation before the low-risk local test, without red flags
only recommends washing the sheets and never tests the skin directly
recommends a water-only rinse after it was reported as failed
recommends friction alone after it was reported to worsen the problem
states that detergent residue (or any listed mechanism) is established
states that firm working necessarily damaged the skin barrier
proposes the useful action only after the user reports discovering it
replaces the natural, no-lye soap with a generic mild soap and claims the exact case was reproduced
recommends an unsafe or injurious self-test
